Field notes: how the machines actually read
The working rules behind every Gerris engagement, stated in the open.
Engines are literal
Google and the AI answer engines take your words at face value. If a phrase is not on the page, in the form buyers actually ask it, the page does not come up for it. There is no thesaurus at the other end, and nobody at Google is inferring what you meant.
Being summarized is mandatory
You do not get to opt out of being described by AI answers. You only choose whether the description is assembled from your facts or from your competitor's.
Consistency is the ranking signal
When your website, your Google Business Profile, and your listings disagree, the answer engine goes with the version it can corroborate. One story, told identically everywhere, is what the machines reward.
Frequently asked questions
What is AEO?
AEO is answer engine optimization. It shapes your website and profiles so AI answer engines (Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini) describe your business accurately and name you in the answer. Search results used to be a list of links. The top of the page is now a written answer, and AEO is the work of earning your place inside it.
What is GEO?
GEO is generative engine optimization. It makes your business easy for generative AI systems to find, understand, verify, and cite: consistent facts across your site and profiles, entity schema, clear direct answers, and pages the crawlers can read. GEO and AEO rest on the same foundation as SEO.
How much does an AI visibility audit cost?
$750 flat. The audit runs 24 buyer questions, the questions buyers actually ask, in their words, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, and Claude, checks the answers' sources against your homepage and up to five money pages, and delivers a written report with every fix in priority order, in five business days. The report is yours to keep regardless of what follows.
What does the Claim Sprint include?
A technical foundation (full crawl, Search Console review, titles and metas, broken links and redirects) and the claim layer (entity schema with sameAs links, llms.txt, a canonical page that states what your business is, and FAQ schema). Items that belong with your developers come back as a precise written fix list. The sprint is scoped from the audit and costs $1,500 flat for the defined scope; work beyond that scope is priced in writing before it begins.
Do I still need SEO if I do AEO?
Yes. AI answers are assembled from crawlable pages, search indexes, business profiles, and directory listings. A site search engines cannot crawl or understand starves the answer engines too. Gerris treats SEO as the foundation and AEO and GEO as the work built on it.
Who is accountable for the work at Gerris?
Chris Abraham. The audit, the strategy, and the measurement are his, and every deliverable arrives in writing under his name. What you buy at Gerris is his judgment about how your business appears in AI search, delivered as finished products: the report, the repaired record, the monthly receipt.

AI Presence is $500 a month, shaped around your search set.
Why does the Google Business Profile matter to AI answers?
For local and service businesses, the Google Business Profile is one of the primary sources AI answers are built from. A suspended, duplicate, or miscategorized profile damages your map listing and corrupts what the AI says about you everywhere else. Gerris profile work, including service-area configuration and reinstatement support, is fulfilled through the practice's Google Business Profile specialist partner and directed by Chris alongside the search work, so your profile, your website, and your listings tell one consistent story. That consistency is what the machines reward.
Why is Google not indexing my pages?
Indexing is where the repair work starts, because a page outside the index is invisible to search results and AI answers alike. Search Console states the symptoms in plain language: crawled, currently not indexed; discovered, currently not indexed; alternate page with proper canonical tag; soft 404. Each message has a cause: crawl budget spent on junk URLs, canonical signals that contradict each other, thin or duplicated templates, a sitemap advertising pages the site itself disowns, responses that waste the crawler’s visit. Chris reads the evidence in Search Console, traces the cause to the template, component, or setting behind it, and repairs the cause rather than resubmitting URLs and hoping.
The diagnosis comes first, inside the opening conversation, before any paid work: it is how Chris decides whether the repair can be made to work, and owners have never paid him for that read. Owners pay for the repair itself, and the ladder below is the published price list for it.
How much does SEO repair cost?
Repair work carries published prices, because its scope can be stated before the work starts:
One-problem repair: $500. One defined problem—an indexing block, a broken redirect chain, a canonical conflict—diagnosed, repaired, and verified in Search Console.
Whole-site repair: $750. The full site read end to end: crawl, index coverage, canonicals, redirects, sitemap, and schema, with every fault found either repaired or returned as a written fix list for your developers.
Large jobs: scoped in milestones. Migrations, multi-site estates, and recoveries are divided into milestones, each one priced in writing before it begins, so a large job is a series of settled decisions instead of one open meter.
What SEO does Gerris do?
The foundation, practiced since 1998:
Technical SEO audits: every URL crawled, each problem traced to the template, component, or script behind it, fixed at the cause, then crawled again to prove it held.
Indexing repair: the dedicated work above, from single blocked pages to a site whose index coverage has collapsed.
Migrations and redirects: full URL inventories, one-to-one 301 maps, launch-day checks, recovery after a move that already lost traffic.
Schema and entities: structured data that validates, matches the visible page, and ties your organization, people, and locations together.
Speed: Core Web Vitals diagnosis, image and script cleanup, caching, and Cloudflare rules that still welcome crawlers.
Measurement setup: Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, and GA4, verified and owned by you.
Can Gerris help our business use AI well?
Yes, as advice from the same seat as the search work. Chris consults on how a business presents itself to AI and how its own people work with AI:
AI integration on your website: where AI features belong on a site, what they should say, and how they read to visitors and to the answer engines watching the same pages.
Technical SEO for AI readers: image alt text, page titles, and meta descriptions written so AI systems describe your pages accurately when they summarize and cite them.
AI tools, training, and best practices: choosing the tools worth paying for, an AI use policy your staff can follow, and training that teaches your team to publish content the engines can read, verify, and cite.
AI inclusion: getting your business into the answers and into the record underneath them—profiles, listings, structured data, and the sources AI systems retrieve from.
The advisory work is consulting: Chris’ judgment on your presence and your practice. Your team keeps its own tools and does its own publishing, with his guidance on what good looks like.

# GitHub Pages Websites: https://gerris.ai/services/github-pages-websites/

Home › Services › GitHub Pages websites
GitHub Pages websites: fast static sites built for AI search
A GitHub Pages website is a complete website made of plain HTML files, hosted free on GitHub, and handed to its owner outright. Gerris designs and builds them for businesses that need a real website—one that loads fast, states their facts clearly, and reads cleanly to the AI answer engines—without a content management system to feed, patch, and defend. The product is the finished site: your domain, your repository, your files, with the claim layer for AI search built into the first page rather than bolted on later.
What is a GitHub Pages website?
GitHub Pages is GitHub’s hosting service for static websites. The site lives in a repository as finished pages: HTML, styles, and images, served directly to every visitor who asks. There is no database behind it, no server-side code, and no admin panel to secure. Your domain points at it, HTTPS is included, and the repository itself is the website in a form any developer can pick up and work on. Ownership is literal: whoever holds the repository holds the site.
That simplicity is the entire design. A conventional website is a machine that assembles pages on demand, and the machine needs fuel, updates, and guarding for as long as it runs. A static site skips the machine. The pages already exist, complete, and the host hands them over. For the brochure-shaped web—service firms, practices, portfolios, publications, and local businesses whose site exists to be found, read, and believed—the finished page is all the machinery the job requires.
Why do static websites load so fast?
A dynamic site builds each page at the moment of the request: database queries, a chain of plugins, a theme rendering the result. A static site does none of that work at request time, because the page was finished before anyone asked for it. A visitor asks for a page and gets the page. Speed here is structural, a property of what the site is, and it shows up everywhere speed is measured: Core Web Vitals scores, the share of your site a crawler can fetch in one visit, and the patience of a buyer on a phone.
The same structure removes the usual failure list. There are no plugins to fall out of date, no database to corrupt, no login page for attackers to knock on. The maintenance a static site asks for is the maintenance of its facts: services, prices, people, and places, kept current the way your Google Business Profile is kept current.
Why is a static site the right shape for AI search?
AI answer engines read the public web, and plain HTML is the easiest material they are ever handed: complete pages that any crawler can fetch end to end, with the facts stated in text rather than locked inside scripts or images. Gerris builds every site to be read that way. Chris calls the goal AI catnip: pages the answer engines find effortless to read, verify, and quote.
The claim layer goes in at the build, as part of the product:
Entity schema: structured data that ties the business to its profiles, its people, and its services as one entity, with sameAs links the engines use to corroborate the record.
An llms.txt file: a plain text statement of who the business is and where its key pages live, written for language models the way a sitemap is written for search crawlers.
Question-led pages: headings in the form buyers ask their questions, with the answer stated directly under each one, in the buyer’s own words for the service and the place.
FAQ content with matching schema: real questions answered on the visible page, in sentences an engine can lift without rewriting them.
A welcoming robots.txt and a clean sitemap: the AI crawlers invited by name, and every page on the site accounted for in the index.
A business that launches with this layer in place starts its AI record as the author of it. The engines summarize every business they can find; a site built this way hands them the summary, in the business’s own facts, from the first day.
What does a Gerris build include?
The delivered product is the complete, launched website:
Design and pages: the layout, the page set, and the copy structure—category stated plainly, services in buyer language, one canonical statement of what the business is.
The claim layer: entity schema, FAQ schema, llms.txt and llms-full.txt, sitemap, and robots.txt, as described above.
Domain and DNS: the domain connected, the records set, HTTPS live.
Measurement in the owner’s name: Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools, and analytics registered to you, so the evidence about your site belongs to you.
Launch verification: the finished site checked the way the engines will meet it—crawlable, indexed, consistent with your Google Business Profile and listings.
This site is one of the builds. gerris.ai runs on GitHub Pages with its llms.txt and schema in the open, and everything claimed on this page can be inspected on it directly.
Can I update the website myself?
Yes. Self-service is part of the product, and it is why the handover is outright. The files are plain HTML in your repository. You can update the text in your own voice, with your own prompts and tools, whenever the facts change—a new service, a new hire, a new location—and the site republishes as fast as you can save the file. Any developer can work on it too; nothing is locked inside a builder that only Gerris can open, and no monthly fee keeps your own website available to you. For changes you would rather hand over, and for the ongoing AI visibility work the site was built to support, Gerris remains on call.
What does a GitHub Pages website cost?
The build is scoped and priced in writing before work begins, in conversation; it is not one of the published-price offers. The running costs are the short list: hosting on GitHub Pages is free, and the domain costs about $10 a year, paid by you directly to the registrar. There are no licence fees, no plugin subscriptions, and no hosting bill.
Which websites do not belong on GitHub Pages?
Online stores with large catalogues and checkout, web applications, and membership sites with logged-in areas need platforms built for those jobs. Chris says so on the opening call when a project points that way. A static site is the right answer for the site most businesses actually need: the one that states what they do, where they do it, and why a buyer should call—and that the answer engines can read as easily as the buyer can.
Frequently asked questions
Is GitHub Pages hosting really free?
Yes. GitHub serves static websites from a repository at no charge. Your running costs are the domain, about $10 a year paid to your registrar, and any changes you commission after launch.
Can AI answer engines read a GitHub Pages website?
Yes, plainly. The pages are finished HTML that any crawler can fetch end to end, and Gerris builds in entity schema, an llms.txt file, and question-led pages from the first day, so Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini read the same record your visitors do.
What happens when I want changes later?
You own the repository, so you can edit the files yourself, hand them to any developer, or ask Gerris to make the change. Nothing about the site depends on Gerris staying in the room.
Is a GitHub Pages website good for a local business?
Yes. The site states the services, the service area, and the facts the Google Business Profile repeats, and that one consistent record feeds the map results and the AI answers alike.

# Guide: What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?: https://gerris.ai/guides/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/

Home › Guides › What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?
What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?
Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the work of getting AI answers to name your business and describe it accurately. When a buyer asks Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Gemini who to hire, the answer names specific businesses and describes what they do, where they are, and what they charge. AEO shapes your website and your profiles so that description is built from your facts, stated in the language your buyers actually use, and so your business is one of the names the answer gives.
What does an answer engine do with your business?
An answer engine reads the web the way a diligent researcher does, then writes a summary. It gathers your website, your Google Business Profile, your directory listings, your reviews, and pages other people have published about you. It resolves those sources into one record of your business, then answers the buyer's question from that record. The summary is mandatory: you do not get to opt out of being described by AI answers. You only choose whether the description is assembled from your facts or from your competitor's.
That assembly happens whether or not your business participates. A firm that has never thought about AI search already has an AI description, written from whatever the engines could find. If your website says one thing about your services and your profile says another, the engine goes with the version it can corroborate, and the version it can corroborate may be the stale one. AEO is the work of taking authorship of that record before the engines finish writing it without you.
What does AEO change on a website?
On the site itself, AEO changes how facts are stated and structured:
A canonical page that states what the business is: the category, the services, the place, and the prices where prices are public, said once, plainly, in one place the engines can point to.
Question-led headings and direct answers: pages written in the form buyers ask their questions, with the answer stated at the top of the section instead of buried under a paragraph of throat clearing.
Entity schema: structured data that connects the organization, its people, and its services as one entity, with sameAs links to the profiles that are also that entity.
FAQ content that answers real questions: the questions buyers ask, answered in plain language on the visible page, with FAQ schema that matches the visible text word for word.
An llms.txt file: a plain text statement of who the business is and where its key pages are, written for language models the way a sitemap is written for search crawlers.
A sound technical foundation: pages crawlers can fetch, an index free of canonical conflicts and dead redirects, and a site that loads fast enough to be read.
None of this is decoration. Each item is a source the answer is assembled from, made legible. A page that states its category only inside an image, or only in words no buyer would type, is a source the engine cannot use, and sources the engine cannot use might as well not exist.
What does AEO change off the website?
Half the record lives off your site, and AEO works there too. The Google Business Profile is a primary source for local and service businesses: its category, services, hours, and service area feed the answer directly. Directory listings and review profiles repeat your name, address, and phone number, and the engines cross-check them against your site. Professional profiles, industry directories, and association pages corroborate who you are and what you do. AEO inventories all of it, finds where the facts disagree, and brings every source into line with the canonical statement on your website.
The disagreement is usually mundane. A business moves and updates its website but not its listings. A profile keeps an old phone number, a shortened name, or a category chosen a decade ago for a service the business no longer sells. Each conflict is small. Together they blur the record, and a blurred record is what makes an answer engine describe you vaguely, describe your competitor instead, or leave your name out of the answer entirely.
How is AEO different from SEO?
SEO earns a place in a list of links. AEO earns a place inside a written answer. A business could live with ranking third under the old arrangement, because the searcher still saw three names and clicked around. The new arrangement puts a written answer at the top of the page that often names two businesses and stops. Ranking below the answer still has value, and the list still gets clicks, but the answer is the first description most buyers now read, and for a growing share of questions it is the only one.
The foundation is shared. AI answers are assembled from crawlable pages, search indexes, business profiles, and listings, so the crawling, indexing, and speed work of SEO is the floor AEO stands on. The difference is the unit of work. SEO optimizes a page for a query. AEO optimizes the whole record the answer is assembled from, across every source the engine reads, in the words the buyer used to ask.
How do you measure AEO?
You measure it the way the buyer experiences it: by asking. Take the searches that bring you revenue, phrased the way buyers phrase them, and put them to Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. Write down what the answers say. Are you named? Are you described accurately, in your category, in your place? Who is named instead of you, and what does the answer claim they do? That written record is the baseline.
Then repeat it on a schedule, because AI answers drift. Competitors publish, directories change, profiles get edited, and the answer that named you in March may name someone else in June. A single screenshot is a snapshot. A monthly series of the same questions, answered in writing, is a measurement, and it is the only honest way to know whether the work is holding.
Where do you start with AEO?
Start by reading your own description. Ask the answer engines about your business today, in your buyers' words, and write down what they say before you change anything. Then fix the record: one canonical statement of what the business is, repeated identically on the website, the profile, and the listings, with pages that answer buyer questions in buyer language. Gerris sells exactly this sequence as the AI Visibility Audit and the Claim Sprint, and the companion guide explains the selection process the audit measures.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between AEO and SEO?
SEO earns a place in the list of links a search engine returns. AEO earns a place inside the written answer an AI engine gives above that list. The two share a foundation: crawlable pages, consistent facts, and clear statements of what a business does. AEO adds the record the answer is assembled from, including business profiles, directory listings, and entity schema.
Does AEO replace SEO?
No. AI answers are assembled from crawlable pages, search indexes, business profiles, and directory listings, so a site search engines cannot crawl or understand starves the answer engines too. AEO is built on SEO. A business doing AEO without the SEO foundation is decorating a house that has no frame.
How long does AEO take to change an AI answer?
The sources can be fixed, and the answers change on the engines' own schedule as they recrawl and rebuild. Gerris measures monthly because a single check proves nothing: the receipt that matters is the trend across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot, and across Claude Code and Codex, over successive months.
What does AEO cost?
At Gerris, the first step is the AI Visibility Audit at $750 flat, delivered as a written report. The Claim Sprint that follows is $1,500 flat for the scope the audit defines, and AI Presence, the monthly measurement, is $500 a month. Work beyond a published scope is priced in writing before it begins.

# Guide: What is generative engine optimization (GEO)?: https://gerris.ai/guides/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/

Home › Guides › What is generative engine optimization (GEO)?
What is generative engine optimization (GEO)?
Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of making a business easy for generative AI systems to find, understand, verify, and cite. A generative engine does not return ten links and stop. It reads sources, resolves them into a record of each business it finds, and writes an answer in its own words that names the businesses the answer rests on. GEO is the discipline of being one of those sources: present in the index, legible to the reader, corroborated by the other sources, and quotable in the answer.
What is a generative engine?
A generative engine is a system that writes its answer instead of only ranking other people's pages. Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini are the four your buyers use most. Each combines retrieval, the fetching of candidate sources from a search index and the live web, with a language model that composes the reply. Classic search ended with a list a human had to read. A generative engine reads the list, and several pages under it, and hands the human a finished paragraph with names in it.
That last step is why the discipline exists. The paragraph is generated, and generation has inputs. A business that appears in the inputs with clear, corroborated facts has a chance of appearing in the paragraph. A business that is absent from the inputs, or present only as confused fragments, is written out of the answer before the answer is written.
How does a generative engine find a business?
Finding starts with crawling. Search crawlers and AI crawlers fetch your pages and build the indexes retrieval draws from. OpenAI sends GPTBot and its search crawlers, Anthropic sends ClaudeBot, Perplexity sends PerplexityBot, and Google and Microsoft read your site for search and for the AI surfaces built on search. robots.txt governs all of them. A site that blocks the AI crawlers, whether by decision or by a copied template default, has removed itself from those engines' sources.
Finding also runs on material gathered earlier. Language models carry a training record of the public web, and a business described consistently for years sits inside that record. Live retrieval corrects and updates the training record only when current sources are reachable. A business that changed its name, its category, or its address has two records running until the live sources are strong enough to settle which one the engine should repeat.
How does a generative engine verify a business?
Verification is corroboration. A fact stated on your website carries more weight when the same fact appears on your Google Business Profile, your listings, and independent pages that mention you. The engine is resolving many sources into one entity record, and it trusts the version of each fact that the sources agree on. Consistency is therefore not tidiness. It is the mechanism by which a fact becomes usable.
Structured data plays a specific role here. Entity schema on your pages declares, in machine-readable form, that this organization is the same one named on those profiles, that this person leads it, and that these are its services and prices. Schema does not replace the visible page, and on this site it is never allowed to say anything the visible page does not say. It confirms the page, in a form the resolver can read without guessing, and confirmed facts are the ones that survive into the generated answer.
How does a generative engine cite a business?
Citation takes two forms. Some engines print their sources: Perplexity and Google AI Overviews show the pages behind the answer, and being the cited page is direct evidence of use. Other surfaces name businesses inside the generated text with no link attached, and on those surfaces being named is the citation that matters, because the name is what the buyer acts on.
Both forms reward the same property: citability. A fact stated plainly, in one place, in the language of the question is liftable. A fact implied across three pages, visible only inside an image, or contradicted somewhere else on the site is not. Direct-answer blocks, honest FAQ content, published prices, and an llms.txt file all exist to make a business's facts liftable. The engine quotes what it can quote, and summarizes the rest from whoever stated it clearly.
What does GEO change in practice?
The working checklist behind every Gerris engagement follows the pipeline in order:
Find: AI crawlers welcomed by name in robots.txt, pages fetchable as plain HTML, a sitemap and an llms.txt that tell every crawler where the record lives.
Understand: a canonical page stating the category, services, place, and prices, with question-led headings and direct answers in the words buyers use.
Verify: entity schema with sameAs links, and the same name, address, phone, category, and services on the website, the Google Business Profile, and the listings.
Cite: facts written in liftable form, FAQ answers that say something specific, and third-party sources that repeat the same story.
Measure: the money questions re-asked across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot, and across Claude Code and Codex, on a monthly schedule, with the answers recorded in writing.
How is GEO different from AEO and SEO?
The three terms describe layers of one foundation, and Gerris keeps the distinction simple. SEO gets a page found and ranked by search engines: crawling, indexing, speed, and structure. GEO gets a business found, verified, and cited by generative systems: the pipeline this guide describes. AEO gets the business named, accurately, inside the answer that results, and the AEO guide covers that layer. A business rarely needs one layer without the others, because the answer is built from the index, the index is built from the crawl, and the crawl reads the same site your customers do.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between GEO and AEO?
GEO is about the pipeline: whether generative AI systems can find your business, understand what it is, verify its facts, and cite it. AEO is about the result: whether the written answer names your business and describes it accurately. The work overlaps almost completely, and a business that does one without the other usually has a gap in the record somewhere.
Do AI crawlers need permission to read my website?
Yes, in effect. Crawlers such as GPTBot, ClaudeBot, and PerplexityBot follow robots.txt, and many business websites block them by accident through copied templates or firewall defaults. A blocked crawler means your pages are absent from that engine's sources. Gerris welcomes the AI crawlers by name on this site and checks the same setting on every client site.
What is llms.txt?
llms.txt is a plain text file at the root of a website that states, in machine-readable text, what the business is, what it sells, and where the key pages are. It is written for language models the way a sitemap is written for search crawlers. This site publishes one, and the Claim Sprint builds one for clients.
How do I know if a generative engine can verify my business?
Ask it. Put your business's category and city into ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews and read what comes back: named or missing, facts right or wrong, competitors named instead. Then check whether your website, Google Business Profile, and listings tell the same story. Disagreement among those sources is the usual reason verification fails.

# Guide: How do AI answers choose which businesses to name?: https://gerris.ai/guides/how-ai-answers-choose-businesses/

Home › Guides › How do AI answers choose which businesses to name?
How do AI answers choose which businesses to name?
An AI answer names the businesses it can assemble a confident description of. Between the buyer's question and the written answer, the engine retrieves sources, resolves them into a record of each candidate business, and composes the answer from the records it trusts. A business with a consistent, corroborated, citable record gets named. A business with a thin or contradictory record gets skipped, and the answer names a competitor whose record lines up. This guide walks through that selection, step by step, because the selection is the thing the AI Visibility Audit measures.
What happens between the question and the answer?
Four things, in order. First, retrieval: the engine fetches candidate pages and profiles for the question from its indexes and the live web. Second, resolution: it works out which mentions belong to the same business, the same person, the same place. Third, corroboration: it compares the resolved records across sources and settles on the facts the sources support. Fourth, composition: the language model writes the answer, naming the businesses whose settled records fit the question.
Notice what is missing from that sequence: a ranking, of the kind the old results page showed. A business can sit in the retrieved set, even rank well as a link, and still never reach the answer, because composition works from records, not links. The question the buyer asked is answered from whatever the engine could assemble, and assembly is where most businesses are lost.
What is an entity record?
Your entity record is everything the engine has gathered and attributed to your business as one entity: its name, its category, its services, its location and service area, its hours, its phone number, its prices where they are published, the people who run it, its profiles, its reviews, and the mentions of it on other sites. The record exists whether or not you have ever looked at it. It was assembled from your website, your Google Business Profile, your listings, and third-party pages, in whatever order the crawlers found them.
Entity schema is how a business takes part in its own record. Schema with a stable identifier and sameAs links declares that this website, this profile, and this listing are the same entity, and states the entity's facts in machine-readable form that matches the visible page. The GEO guide describes the verification pipeline in full. Without that declaration, resolution is guesswork, and the engine's guesses about which mentions belong to you are exactly as good as the mess it was handed.
Why does consistency decide who gets named?
Because corroboration is a vote, and consistency is how a fact wins it. When your website, your Google Business Profile, and your listings disagree, the answer engine goes with the version it can corroborate. Three sources stating the same category, the same services, and the same phone number outweigh one louder source stating something else. The engine is not judging which version is true. It is reporting which version it could verify.
The failures are concrete. The website calls the business a plumber, the profile calls it a handyman service, and an old listing calls it a general contractor: three blurred records instead of one clear one. The address changed in one place and not the others. The founding service, the one buyers ask about, appears on a brochure site and nowhere the crawlers go. Each blur costs confidence, and the answer's names are the businesses that cost it the least. This is also why the fix is unglamorous. Consistency is a ranking signal precisely because it is work most businesses never finish.
What makes a business easy to cite?
Citability is a property of how facts are written down. A canonical page that states what the business is, in the category language buyers search, gives the engine one authoritative source to resolve everything else against. Direct answers in buyer language, stated at the top of the page section that answers them, can be lifted into an answer without rewriting. Published prices, where the business can publish them, settle questions competitors leave vague. FAQ content answers the follow-up questions. An llms.txt file hands the whole record to language models in one plain text document.
None of this asks the engine for a favor. The engine is under pressure to answer quickly and defensibly, and it reaches for the sources that cost it the least effort and the least risk. A business whose facts arrive pre-assembled, consistently, in quotable sentences is simply the easiest correct answer available. Being good at the work matters after the buyer calls. Getting named is a clerical contest held before that, and it is won on the quality of the paperwork.
What makes an AI answer skip a business?
The skip list, from the audits, is repetitive:
Crawlers blocked: robots.txt or a firewall default keeps the AI crawlers out, so the pages never enter the sources.
No plain statement of category: no page says, in so many words, what the business is and what it sells, so retrieval finds nothing to resolve.
Contradictory facts: the website, profile, and listings tell different stories, and corroboration fails on the details that matter.
A broken profile: a suspended, duplicate, or miscategorized Google Business Profile corrupts the record at one of its primary sources.
Facts locked in unreadable forms: the key statements live inside images, scripts, or documents the engines read poorly, if at all.
No third-party corroboration: nothing anywhere repeats the business's own claims, so every fact rests on a single source.
Read the list again and notice what it does not contain: the quality of the business's work. Skips are record problems. The engine is not reporting that a competitor is better at your trade. It is reporting that a competitor's paperwork assembled more cleanly, and paperwork can be fixed.
How do you find out what the answers say about you?
You run the questions yourself, before you fix anything. Take the searches that bring you revenue, ask them in Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini in the words your buyers use, and write down what comes back: named or skipped, described rightly or wrongly, and who was named in your place. Then compare the answers against your record, find the disagreements and the gaps, fix them in priority order, and re-run the same questions monthly to confirm the answers moved.
That test, run properly and written down, is the AI Visibility Audit on the Gerris services page. It is $750 flat. We run 24 buyer questions, the questions buyers actually ask, in their words, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, and Claude, check the answers' sources against your homepage and up to five money pages and your entity and name, address, and phone consistency, and deliver a written report with every fix in priority order, in five business days. The report is yours to keep regardless of what follows.
Frequently asked questions
Why does ChatGPT recommend my competitor instead of me?
Usually because the competitor's record is easier to assemble: their category, services, and location are stated plainly on a page the engine can read, and the same facts appear on their Google Business Profile and listings. The engine names the business it can describe with confidence. The fix is rarely one trick. It is making your record as consistent and citable as theirs.
What is an entity in AI search?
An entity is one real-world thing the engine tracks as a single record: a business, a person, a place, a service. Your business's entity record is everything the engine has gathered about it from your website, your profiles, and other sites' mentions. Entity schema with sameAs links tells the engine which pages and profiles belong to the same entity.
Can a business pay to be named in an AI answer?
Not in the organic answers this guide is about. There is no placement to buy inside the written answer. What a business can do is fix the record the answer is built from: consistent facts, a canonical page, readable answers to buyer questions, and profiles that agree. That is the whole of the method, and it is also the product Gerris sells.
How much does it cost to find out what AI answers say about my business?
The AI Visibility Audit is $750 flat. Gerris runs 24 buyer questions, the questions buyers actually ask, in their words, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, and Claude, checks the answers' sources against your homepage and up to five money pages, and delivers a written report with every fix in priority order, in five business days. The report is yours to keep regardless of what follows.

# Blog: How AI engines read your business: literal words, mandatory summaries, consistent facts: https://gerris.ai/blog/how-ai-engines-read-your-business/

Home › Blog › How AI engines read your business
How AI engines read your business: literal words, mandatory summaries, consistent facts
By Chris Abraham, Gerris AI. Published Tuesday, November 17, 2026.
AI engines read your business literally, summarize it whether you take part or not, and name the businesses whose facts agree everywhere the engines look. Those are the three working rules behind every Gerris engagement, and they appear in short form in the field notes on the home page. This post states them at full length: what a literal reader does to your copy, why the summary of your business gets written with or without you, and how consistency across your website, your Google Business Profile, and your listings became the signal that decides whose version of the facts an answer repeats.
What does it mean that the engines read literally?
Google and the AI answer engines take your words at face value. If a phrase is missing from the page, in the form buyers actually ask it, the page does not come up for that phrase. There is no thesaurus at the other end, and nobody at Google is inferring what you meant. A search system matches the words in the question against words it can find in its sources, and the answer engines build on that same matching before they write a single sentence of their own.
This surprises owners who wrote their sites for human readers with patience. A human visitor forgives a home page that calls the firm a solutions provider while the words estate planning attorney sit three clicks deep; the human can guess, browse, and telephone. The engine works from the text it retrieved. Category language that lives in a printed brochure, a trade-show banner, or the owner's head never enters the record, and a record entry that never happened cannot be summarized, cited, or named.
The practical consequence is plain. The words buyers type and speak—emergency plumber near me, CPA for restaurants, who sells standing desks in Austin—have to appear on your pages in those forms, attached to your name, your place, and your prices where prices are public. Synonyms chosen for elegance are a private vocabulary. The engine keeps the buyer's words and discards yours wherever the two differ.
Why does the summary get written whether you take part or not?
Being summarized is mandatory. You do not get to opt out of being described by AI answers. You only choose whether the description is assembled from your facts or from your competitor's.
Every business with a website, a profile, or a single review already has an AI description. The engines assembled it from whatever they could find: the site, the Google Business Profile, directory listings, review pages, and anything third parties published. A firm that has never thought about AI search is participating at full strength; it simply never read its own entry. When a buyer asks who to hire, the answer reads that entry aloud, in the buyer's hearing, at the moment of decision.
This changes what doing nothing costs. Under the old results page, a business that ignored search could still be found by referral and foot traffic while it ignored the list, and the list said nothing about it beyond a title and a line of text. The answer layer speaks about the business either way, in the business's absence, from sources the business may never have read. Authorship of the record is the only choice on offer. Gerris's work starts from that fact: the description exists, so the business may as well write it.
How does an engine decide which version of your facts to repeat?
It goes with the version it can corroborate. An answer engine resolves many sources into one record of your business, and it trusts the version of each fact that the sources agree on. When your website, your Google Business Profile, and your listings state the same category, the same services, and the same phone number, that fact is settled and usable. When the sources disagree, the engine reports the version it could verify, and the version it could verify may be the stale one.
Consistency is a ranking signal in the plainest sense. One story, told identically everywhere, is what the machines reward. The reward is clerical: a fact that survives corroboration can be stated in an answer plainly, and answers are built from facts the engine can state. A fact tangled in contradiction costs the engine confidence, and the answer's names go to the businesses that cost it the least. The guide to how AI answers choose which businesses to name walks through that selection step by step.
What breaks when your website, your profile, and your listings disagree?
The failures are mundane, and the audits meet the same ones every month. The website calls the business a plumber, the profile calls it a handyman service, and an old listing calls it a general contractor: three blurred records where one clear one should stand. The address changed on the site and stayed old in the listings. A phone number from a previous office keeps circulating in the directories. The founding service, the one buyers ask about by name, appears on a printed brochure and nowhere the crawlers go.
Each conflict is small. Together they blur the record, and a blurred record earns a vague description, a description of a competitor, or silence. Read the skip list again and notice what it never contains: the quality of the business's work. The engine reports on paperwork, and paperwork can be fixed. Every item on the skip list has a clerical remedy, and the remedies are the same ones the guide to generative engine optimization sets out in pipeline order.
How should a business write for a literal reader?
The working checklist behind every Gerris engagement follows from the three rules:
State the category in so many words: one canonical page that says what the business is, what it sells, where it works, and what it charges where prices are public.
Write headings as the questions buyers ask: the answer goes directly under each heading, at the top of the section, in the buyer's language.
Repeat the record identically: the same name, address, phone number, category, and services on the website, the profile, and the listings, word for word where the formats allow.
Publish facts in liftable form: direct answers, honest FAQ content, and published prices give the engine sentences it can quote without rewriting them.
Hand the machines the whole record at once: entity schema with sameAs links and an llms.txt file tell every crawler and language model where the canonical statement lives.
None of this is decoration, and none of it asks an engine for a favor. The engine is under pressure to answer quickly and defensibly, and it reaches for the sources that cost it the least effort and the least risk. A business whose facts arrive pre-assembled, consistently, in quotable sentences is simply the easiest correct answer available.
How do you check what the machines say about you today?
You ask, in your buyers' words, and you write down the answers. Put your category and your city to Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. Record whether you are named, whether the description matches your facts, and who is named in your place. Then compare the answers against your website, your profile, and your listings, and find where the record disagrees with itself. That comparison is the diagnosis, and the fixes follow it in priority order.
Gerris sells that test, run properly and written down, as the AI Visibility Audit: the money questions asked across the four engines, the entity and name-address-phone consistency checked, and a written report with every fix in priority order. The guide to answer engine optimization defines the discipline the audit measures, for owners who want the category settled before they buy anything in it.
Frequently asked questions
Do AI engines understand synonyms and implied meaning?
They work from the words on the page. A search system matches the words in the buyer's question against words it can find in its sources, and the answer engines build on that matching. A category stated only in elegant synonyms, or implied by photographs and reputation, is a category the record may never receive. State what the business is in the words buyers use to ask for it.
Can a business stop AI answers from describing it?
The description is assembled from public sources: the website, the Google Business Profile, directory listings, reviews, and pages other people publish. A business can withdraw from some of those sources and shrink what the engines can find, and the answer will then describe it from whatever remains, or name a competitor whose record is complete. The working choice is authorship: write the record yourself, in your own facts, and keep it consistent.
What is the first consistency fix to make?
Settle one canonical statement of the business: the name, the category, the services, the address or service area, and the phone number. Then bring the Google Business Profile and the highest-traffic directory listings into line with that statement, word for word where the formats allow. Most records improve measurably from that single pass, because corroboration starts working for the business instead of against it.
How often do AI answers about a business change?
Continuously, on the engines' own schedule. Competitors publish, directories change, profiles get edited, and the answer that named a business in March may name another in June. A single check is a snapshot. Gerris measures monthly, re-asking the same money questions across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot, and across Claude Code and Codex, because the trend across months is the measurement that can be acted on.

# The AI Search Briefing: https://gerris.ai/briefing/

Home › Briefing
The AI Search Briefing
The AI Search Briefing is a weekly briefing on AI search from Gerris AI: answer engine optimization (AEO), AI optimization (AIO), generative engine optimization (GEO), and what AI is doing to search engine optimization (SEO), written from practice for business owners. Each edition takes the week’s platform changes, published research, and rulings, states in plain language what actually happened and where it was announced, and says why it matters to a business that needs to be named when an AI assistant answers its buyers.
What does each edition cover?
Only AI search. Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT search, Perplexity, and Gemini; AI crawlers and robots.txt rules; and published AEO and GEO research with its method stated. Every item links to the primary announcement or the study itself, and figures a platform reports about itself are labelled as that platform’s own numbers. If an item cannot be tied to a source, it does not run.

# AI Search Briefing: Week of November 7, 2026: https://gerris.ai/briefing/2026-11-07/

Home › Briefing › Week of November 7, 2026
AI Search Briefing: Week of November 7, 2026
By Chris Abraham, Gerris AI. Published Saturday, November 7, 2026.
This edition covers the week to Saturday, November 7, 2026: a Turkish investigation into Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, Google folding AI into school Search, OpenAI merging ChatGPT chat and agent work, two Perplexity releases, and two pieces of field research on AI crawlers. Figures a platform reports about itself are labelled as that platform’s own numbers; nothing here runs without a source.
Can a publisher keep Google AI from using its content without losing search visibility?
Turkey opened a formal investigation into Google AI Overviews and AI Mode on Monday, November 2, and ordered interim terms for news publishers while the case runs. The Turkish Competition Authority (Rekabet Kurumu) says it will examine whether Google abused a dominant position with the two AI features. Its interim measure, decided October 8, requires Google to offer news publishers non-discriminatory terms that reflect the economic value of their content in AI Overviews and AI Mode, and to let each publisher decide how its content is used there without any effect on its visibility or indexing in other Google services. The measure covers news publishers, sets no amount and no deadline, and a parallel European Commission investigation has been open since December 2025.
Why it matters to your business: the argument over whether opting out of AI answers can cost you ordinary search visibility is now a legal case in more than one jurisdiction, not a settings page. If regulators establish that the two decisions are separate, every business gets to make its AI decision on its merits. Watch what the United States does with the same question.
Source: Rekabet Kurumu announcement, November 2, 2026, as reported by Maccus
Is there still a version of Google Search without AI answers?
Google made Search and AI one product for schools this week, and confirmed there is no AI-free version of Search to switch to. In its November 3 post on responsible AI for schools, Google says access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until a school administrator explicitly turns them on, and that its Guided Learning tutoring is built into Search itself, piloting in select U.S. schools later this month and live in Google Classroom worldwide from November 3. Reporting on the announcement adds the structural fact: Google offers no version of Search without AI Overviews or AI Mode, and its education chief told the New York Times that Search and AI are deeply integrated.
Why it matters to your business: any plan that assumes your buyers use a “regular Google” with ten blue links is planning for a product Google no longer ships. The answer layer is the search product now, in the most cautious rollout Google runs, its schools channel. Being named inside the AI answer is the placement to win.
Source: Google, “Responsible AI for schools with Guided Learning,” November 3, 2026
Is ChatGPT becoming an agent that acts, not just an answer box?
OpenAI is merging ChatGPT’s Chat and Work tabs into a single experience. TechCrunch reported November 2 on OpenAI’s email to users: the merged product rolls out first to a small group for feedback, then widely. In one place, a user can bring in files and plugins and have ChatGPT build a website, make a presentation, or act on the web. Codex stays a separate product, and ChatGPT and Codex will draw their usage from the same allowance pool. Anthropic made the same merge for Claude in September.
Why it matters to your business: the assistant your buyers ask is becoming the assistant that books, buys, and builds on their behalf. The next visibility question after “does it name us” is “can its agent complete the job on our site”: clear prices, clear service pages, and forms an agent can finish.
Source: TechCrunch, November 2, 2026
Do automated systems check the live web before they judge your business?
Perplexity’s Decisions API now searches the web before it answers. Announced November 4, a single setting, mode: "web_grounding", makes the API run a live search for each question and answer from the results. In Perplexity’s own test of 328 true-or-false claims, accuracy rose from 56.4% without grounding, close to guessing, to 97.3% with it; on the public PWS-Decisions benchmark it rose from 51% to 86%, with median response time rising from 139 to 366 milliseconds. Each completed search costs $0.001. These are Perplexity’s figures from its own post; no independent rerun has been published.
Why it matters to your business: software that qualifies accounts, checks eligibility, and verifies claims about companies is starting to check the live web first. When it checks yours, the page it finds is your record. A current page with your services, prices, and locations in plain text is what gets read back as fact.
Source: Perplexity, “Web grounding for the Decisions API,” November 4, 2026
What does cheaper agent research mean for your website?
Perplexity cut the cost of its Agent API research at every effort level and added an ultra level for the widest research jobs. Announced November 5: the medium level’s score on the BrowseComp and DSQA research benchmarks rose from 55% to 77% while its cost fell almost 90%; the xhigh level held its WANDR research score at 76.5% at about a quarter of its August 2026 cost; and the new ultra level runs three research agents in parallel with a fourth merging their findings, scoring 85.9% on WANDR at $21.71 per task. All figures are Perplexity’s own. One mechanism matters for site owners: instead of handing an agent your whole page, Perplexity now extracts only the passages relevant to its task and quotes them exactly.
Why it matters to your business: deep research over the open web, including over your site and your competitors’, just got much cheaper, so expect more of it. Answers assembled by agents are built from quoted passages. Pages with quotable, plainly stated facts about what you sell, where, and for how much are the pages that get quoted.
Source: Perplexity, “Improvements to every Agent API effort level,” November 5, 2026
Why is ChatGPT’s crawler visiting your site less while its referrals rise?
ChatGPT opens small business pages 62% less often than it did in July, and sends those sites more visitors than ever. LovedByAI measured 714 small business websites through its WordPress plugin. Page reads by ChatGPT-User, the bot that opens a page while answering, fell from 8,716 a day in late July to 3,344 a day in late October, a 62% drop overall and 66% at the typical site, in three unannounced steps on August 20, September 17–18, and October 28. Over the same span, visitors arriving from ChatGPT links rose 160% in total and 72% at the typical site. The study’s reading, not confirmed by OpenAI, is that ChatGPT answers more questions from what it has already indexed and cached, and fetches live pages less.
Why it matters to your business: judge ChatGPT by the visitors it sends, never by its bot traffic; a quieter crawler in your logs is not lost ground. The stored copy of your site increasingly does the talking at answer time, which makes crawler access and plain-text facts on the page worth more, not less.
Source: LovedByAI Lab, “ChatGPT visits websites less, sends more traffic,” updated November 3, 2026
Should your robots.txt treat training bots and search bots the same?
No, and 9.2% of large sites now write the file that way: training blocked, AI search allowed. Sitecheckly’s November 2026 survey of the Tranco top 10,000 domains, 4,546 of them with a readable robots.txt, found 9.2% block training crawlers while still allowing AI search crawlers. The distinction is real and named: OpenAI’s GPTBot trains models while OAI-SearchBot feeds ChatGPT search; Anthropic’s ClaudeBot trains while Claude-SearchBot searches; Google-Extended is a training control token, not a crawler, and blocking it has no effect on Google Search or AI Overviews.
Why it matters to your business: a blanket “block AI” robots.txt, often pasted in from a template, can lock your business out of AI answers while doing nothing you intended. Write the file as three separate decisions: training, search, and fetch-on-request, and check the published file, not the draft in your editor.
Source: Sitecheckly, “AI Crawlers List: Training vs. Search User Agents,” November 3, 2026
What is Gerris watching next week?
Three threads. Whether Google answers the Turkish interim measure in public, and whether any U.S. proceeding takes up the same opt-out question. Whether ChatGPT-User page reads step down again, which would confirm the index-first pattern the LovedByAI data shows. And whether the merged ChatGPT chat-and-work experience reaches general users, which moves agent readiness from a developer topic to a storefront topic. The next edition runs Saturday, November 14, 2026.
Is your business named when AI answers?
The AI Visibility Audit answers that question for your business, market, and competitors for a flat $750. It checks what ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews say about you today, and what to fix first.

# The AI search glossary: https://gerris.ai/guides/ai-search-glossary/

AI search has produced more acronyms in three years than SEO produced in twenty. GEO, AEO, AIO, LLMO, AXO, SXO, GPTO, and a dozen more turn up in agency pitches, often for the same work under a different name. This glossary defines each one in plain language, says which describe a real method and which are relabels, and adds the technical terms and metrics that come with them. The definitions are checked against primary sources where one exists, listed at the end.
The short version: almost every acronym here means making a business easy for AI systems to find, understand, verify, and cite. Google's own documentation says there are no additional requirements or special optimizations needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no new machine-readable files or markup. Ask anyone who sells one of these acronyms to name the tasks, the evidence they will collect, and how the result will be measured. The tasks matter; the acronym does not.

## The acronyms

Most of these name the same job: getting a business found, described correctly, and cited by AI systems. The differences are usually in who is selling the label.

**AAIO (agentic AI optimization) and AXO (agentic experience optimization)**
Preparing a website for AI agents that act for a person: comparing options, filling forms, booking, buying. The practical work is old-fashioned: real buttons and links, labeled form fields, prices and stock stated in text, and checkout steps a machine can follow. Accessible sites are already most of the way there.

**AEO (answer engine optimization)**
Work aimed at being the answer an AI assistant, voice assistant, or answer box gives to a question. Gerris has a full guide: What is answer engine optimization? (/guides/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/)

**AI SEO and AISO (AI search optimization)**
Broad labels for SEO adapted to AI search, or for SEO done with AI tools. The phrase covers both meanings in the wild, so it says little until the seller describes the actual tasks.

**AIO**
Used two ways. Some agencies mean AI optimization, an umbrella for all AI visibility work; others mean AI Overviews optimization, earning citations in Google's AI Overviews specifically. When someone sells AIO, the first question is which one.

**AVO (AI visibility optimization)**
Another umbrella label for improving how often and how accurately AI answers mention a brand. Functionally the same work as GEO and AEO.

**GAIO (generative AI optimization) and GSO (generative search optimization)**
Alternate names for GEO, used by agencies that wanted a label of their own.

**GEO (generative engine optimization)**
Making a business easy for generative AI systems to find, understand, verify, and cite. The term comes from a research paper of that name by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues, first posted in November 2023 and accepted to KDD 2024, which reported that some content changes raised visibility in generative engine responses by up to 40 percent. Gerris explains the practice in What is generative engine optimization? (/guides/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/)

**GPTO (ChatGPT optimization)**
GEO aimed at one engine. Optimizing for a single assistant is a weak plan when buyers use several, and the underlying work is the same for all of them.

**LLMO (large language model optimization) and LLM SEO**
Shaping what large language models say about a brand: consistent facts, a clear entity, and outside sources a model will trust. In practice it overlaps GEO almost completely.

**Search everywhere optimization**
The idea that visibility now depends on many platforms at once, including YouTube, Reddit, TikTok, Amazon, and the AI assistants, along with Google. The observation is fair: AI answers draw heavily on forums and video. The label adds no new technique.

**SEO (search engine optimization)**
Making a site crawlable, indexable, and worth ranking in search engines. Every AI label above still depends on it, because AI systems retrieve from search indexes and crawled pages.

**SEO 2.0**
A marketing name for SEO that accounts for AI answers. It describes a sales pitch more than a method.

**SIO (search intent optimization)**
Matching pages to what a searcher is trying to do. This has been a core part of SEO for well over a decade under the name search intent.

**SXO (search experience optimization)**
Combining search visibility with the experience after the click: speed, clarity, and a page that answers the question. With AI answers, part of that experience now happens before any click, in the summary itself.

**VEO (voice engine optimization)**
Optimizing for spoken answers from voice assistants. The work is the same as AEO: short, direct answers in plain language, attached to a clear entity.

## The machinery

These terms describe how AI search actually works. They are worth learning, because they explain what a site can and cannot influence.

**Agentic browser**
A browser with an AI agent built in that can carry out multi-step tasks for its user. OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas and Perplexity's Comet are examples. They read pages through the same structure screen readers use, which is why semantic HTML matters to them.

**Agentic RAG**
Retrieval run by an AI agent that decides for itself when to search again, which tools to use, and when it has enough to answer. Deep research features in the major assistants work this way.

**AI crawler**
A bot that fetches web pages for an AI company, either to train models or to answer questions live. OpenAI, for example, runs separate bots for each job and treats each robots.txt setting independently: blocking GPTBot (training) does not block OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search).

**AI Overviews and AI Mode**
Google's two generative search surfaces. AI Overviews is the summary at the top of some results pages, the successor to the Search Generative Experience test; AI Mode is the separate conversational search that uses query fan-out. Google says there are no extra requirements to appear in either beyond ordinary SEO, and their traffic is counted in Search Console's regular Performance report under the Web search type.

**Answer engine**
Any system that replies to a question with a written answer instead of a list of links: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, Claude, and Google's AI Mode among them.

**Chunking**
Splitting a long document into shorter passages so a retrieval system can index and return each one separately. For a website, the lesson is that each section should make sense on its own, with a heading that says what it covers.

**ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, Claude-User, and Claude-Agent**
Anthropic's four user agents. ClaudeBot collects content that may be used for training, Claude-SearchBot improves Claude's search results, Claude-User fetches a page when a person's question needs it, and Claude-Agent identifies the browsers Anthropic hosts for Claude to complete tasks for users. Each can be allowed or blocked separately in robots.txt.

**Embedding (vector embedding)**
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a passage, so a system can find passages close in meaning to a question even when the words differ. Talk of measuring a brand's semantic distance from a prompt describes this math. No website owner can see or set those numbers directly.

**Google-Extended**
A robots.txt product token Google uses to let publishers decide whether crawled content may be used for training Gemini models and for grounding. Google states that it does not affect a site's inclusion in Google Search and is not a ranking signal.

**GraphRAG**
Retrieval over a knowledge graph of entities and relationships instead of, or alongside, similar text passages. Microsoft Research described it in an April 2024 paper by Darren Edge and colleagues: a language model extracts the entities and relationships from a collection, groups closely related entities into communities, summarizes each community, and builds answers from those summaries. It handles questions that span a whole collection or connect several sources better than passage retrieval, and adds little for single-fact lookups. A lighter variant, LazyGraphRAG (November 2024), brought indexing cost down to that of vector retrieval, 0.1 percent of full GraphRAG. It rewards sites whose facts about people, places, and organizations are stated the same way everywhere, because those facts become the nodes.

**Grounding**
Anchoring an AI answer in sources retrieved at the time of the question rather than in training memory alone. Grounded answers are the ones that carry citations, which makes grounding the moment a website can earn a link.

**Grounding queries**
The searches an AI system actually ran while assembling an answer, which often differ from what the user typed. Bing Webmaster Tools now shows a sample of them for pages it cited.

**Hybrid retrieval**
Finding passages two ways at once: keyword matching (the classic method, often BM25) and meaning matching through embeddings, then merging the results. It is why both the exact words buyers use and clear, plain explanations help a page get retrieved.

**llms.txt**
A proposed Markdown file at a site's root that summarizes the site and links its key pages for language models. It is a proposal, and AI companies have not committed to reading it, but it costs little and this site publishes one: gerris.ai/llms.txt (/llms.txt).

**MCP (Model Context Protocol)**
An open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, that lets AI assistants connect to outside tools and data sources in a standard way. For a business, MCP matters when it wants assistants to query its own systems, such as inventory or bookings, directly.

**OAI-SearchBot**
OpenAI's crawler for ChatGPT's search features. OpenAI says blocking it keeps a site out of ChatGPT search answers, though the site can still appear as a navigational link.

**Query fan-out**
Google's own term for how AI Mode works: it breaks a question into subtopics and issues many searches at once on the user's behalf, then writes one answer from the results. Google described it in May 2025. A page can be cited for a subquestion the user never typed.

**RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)**
A design in which a system first retrieves relevant passages from an index, then has a language model write its answer from them, usually with citations. The approach was named in a 2020 research paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues. AI search assistants are RAG systems built on web indexes. Retrieval is the weak point: when the wrong passages come back, the answer is wrong with full confidence, which is why being the clearest, most retrievable source on a question matters more than being one of many.

**Reranker**
A second model that rescores the top passages a retriever found and puts the most relevant first, before the answer is written. Passages that answer the question directly tend to survive reranking.

## Content and authority

These describe what makes a source worth citing. Most are new names for what good publishers and good PR have always done.

**Answer blocks and passage-level optimization**
Writing each section so it stands alone: a heading phrased as the question, and a direct answer in the first sentence or two beneath it. AI systems lift passages, and a passage that needs the paragraph before it to make sense gets skipped.

**Attribute list**
The short set of facts and differentiators a business wants AI answers to repeat about it: what it does, where, for whom, and what sets it apart. Writing one down is useful, because consistency across the web is what lets engines repeat it.

**Brand co-occurrence**
How often a brand's name appears near the topics, places, and descriptions it wants to be known for, on sites other than its own. It is the AI-era name for being mentioned in the right company, which is earned through press, reviews, and community, and cannot be faked at scale without risk.

**Claim layer**
Gerris' name for the structured statements a business publishes about itself so machines can read them directly: entity schema, FAQ markup, llms.txt, and one canonical description of what the business is.

**Entity**
A specific, identifiable thing, such as a person, business, product, or place, that search engines and AI systems track as one item across many sources. Entity-first SEO means making sure every source describes the same entity the same way.

**FAQ markup**
FAQPage structured data. Google deprecated the FAQ rich result and stopped showing it in Search on May 7, 2026, so the markup no longer earns an expanded listing. It still describes a page's questions and answers in a form any machine can read, and the questions themselves remain useful on the visible page.

**Information gain and non-commodity content**
What a page adds that other pages on the topic do not: original data, first-hand experience, a tested method, a named expert. Pages with something new to say have a reason to be cited; pages that restate the consensus do not. Google has described the same quality as content that is original and non-commodity.

**Knowledge graph**
A database of entities and the relationships between them. Google's Knowledge Graph feeds its knowledge panels, and AI systems build similar structures. Knowledge graph alignment means your schema, profiles, and listings all agree.

**Prompt-to-publish loop**
Researching the questions buyers put to AI assistants and publishing pages that answer them. This is keyword research with longer queries, and it works best when each answer lives on one page instead of many near-duplicates.

## The metrics

Measurement in AI search is young, and every tool measures a sample. These terms are useful when the method behind them is stated.

**AI citation rate**
The share of answers, across a fixed set of questions, that link to or footnote your domain. It only means something when the question set, engines, dates, and location are written down and repeated the same way.

**AI Performance (Bing Webmaster Tools)**
A report Microsoft introduced in public preview on February 10, 2026. It shows how often a site is cited as a source in Microsoft Copilot and in AI-generated summaries in Bing: total citations, the average number of cited pages, per-URL citation counts, and sampled grounding queries. See how to read Bing’s AI Performance report (/guides/bing-ai-performance-report/).

**Cross-model visibility**
How consistently a brand appears across different AI systems, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, and Copilot. Engines draw on different sources, so a brand can be named by one and missing from another.

**Hallucination rate**
How often AI answers state something false about a business: wrong prices, closed locations, invented services. Every wrong fact has a source or a gap behind it, and tracing that source is the start of the fix.

**Mention rate**
How often an AI answer names a brand, with or without a link. Mentions and citations are separate measures: a brand can be named without its site being cited, and a site can be cited for a fact without the brand being recommended.

**Prompt monitoring, prompt panels, and prompt volume**
Tools that run a fixed set of questions through AI assistants on a schedule and record the answers. A prompt panel is that question set; prompt volume is an estimate of how often people ask something similar. Volume figures are modeled estimates, since no AI company publishes query counts the way search engines publish keyword data.

**Share of model and share of answer**
The AI version of share of voice: how often an assistant names your brand compared with competitors across a set of prompts. Because answers vary from run to run, a single check proves little; repeated, dated runs show the trend.

**Zero-click visibility**
Presence in answers that users read without visiting any website. Rankings and mentions can grow while clicks fall, so reports should track both.

## Which of these names real work?

Three ideas carry the weight. The first is that AI systems retrieve from search indexes and crawled pages, so technical SEO still decides whether a site can be found at all. The second is that answers are assembled from many sources, so the facts on a business's own site, its Google Business Profile, its listings, and the press about it have to agree. The third is that citations go to pages with something worth citing: original evidence, clear answers, and an identifiable author. Every acronym above is a way of packaging some part of those three.
For the measurement side, the guide to how AI answers choose which businesses to name (/guides/how-ai-answers-choose-businesses/) walks through the entity record, the consistency check, and the citability test. For definitions of traditional SEO terms, such as canonical tags, crawl budget, and soft 404s, see the glossaries on christopherabraham.com (https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/) and gerriscorp.com (https://gerriscorp.com/guides/glossary/).
